utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Geoffrey Nice, Kenneth Scott, Susan Somers, and Patrick Lopez-Terres; case manager, Alinde Ver Haag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the Kordic defence, Your Honour, Turner Smith and Mr. Mitko Naumovski, my co-counsel, and two colleagues that I would like to introduce to you, Mr. Stephen Sayers from our firm and Mr. Bob Stein from the firm of Stein, Volinsky, and Callaghan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. President. Counsel for the accused Mario Cerkez, Bozidar Kovacic, attorney from Rijeka, and may I introduce my assistant, Mr. Pavlekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVLEKOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, Your Honours, I should, first of all, like to address the Court in Croatian, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVLEKOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I am attorney Vladimir Pavlekovic from Zagreb, and I have a private practice there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want to ensure the accused can hear in a language which they understand. THE ACCUSED KORDIC: (Interpretation) Thank you once again for your kindness and understanding. Yes, I do understand Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED CERKEZ: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. I understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, the purpose of this hearing is essentially a pre-trial conference with this case listed to start next month. The matters which are outstanding, which I have in mind to deal with today, are, first of all, a motion for provisional release, and we will hear any submissions which any party may wish to make on that; questions then of readiness for trial; the status of disclosure and discovery; next, then the Rule 73 bis requirements, and we will go through that Rule in due course; the remaining motions, which have very recently been filed, which I hope at least we can discuss, they involve a motion about trial procedure from the Prosecution filed two days ago; the status of agreed facts and admissions, if any. There is a Defence motion concerning the advance notice of evidence obtained during a search. Again, it may be that we can discuss that. Finally, a timetable for trial and any useful rulings we can make in relation to the trial. We have all day for this hearing, although I hope we can deal with the matters this morning. If there comes a time when there are matters which the parties wish to discuss, of course, they shall have time to do so during the day. That is the proposed timetable agenda for the hearing. Before we start, are there any matters which anybody wishes to raise at the very outset about that timetable agenda? Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would respectfully suggest that we put the suggestion of provisional release at some point in the discussions after the discussion of readiness for trial and Rule 73 bis requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Seems sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us then move to the position of readiness for trial. It may be as well to start with matters of discovery and what the state of discovery is, at the same time having open Rule 73 bis which deals with pre-trial conferences. Yes. Mr. Nice, we have your notice of compliance of the 5th of March with the Rules. In due course, we shall have to return to the witness list and how that is to be dealt with, but at this stage, is it your position that apart from one or two matters and one or two witnesses that there may be -- by "one or two" I mean a number but not a substantial number or anything like that -- you have complied with all the requirements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There is a problem about translation, and I can bring the Court up to date with that position. There is an additional list of witnesses which I have already distributed to my learned friends. I will make that available immediately to Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues. It has itself to be slightly corrected today, but the computer system was not functioning at the time one or two entries were sought. There is the question of summaries which has been raised by my learned friends yesterday in a meeting that we had together. Perhaps I can deal with those issues now? Summaries first. Seventy-three suggests or requires, it depends how you view it, that at the service of the list of witnesses, there should also be summaries provided. I first raised this matter with the Court a long time ago and explained to the Court that practices as to summaries varied and asked the Court if it would indicate what it would desire. At the next hearing, although we dealt with the timing of a witness list, I overlooked to repeat my request to the Court as to what it would most wish by way of summaries. Since then, there have been some informal discussions through the usual channels about either summaries or the possibility of the Court working on full witness statements, which is certainly the course preferred by one of the Chambers in the Tribunal, or maybe more than one. So summaries have not been provided with this witness list, although it is true to say that an updated and improved version of the list, which will again be served when one or two other matters have been researched through the computer system, assuming it is working, will at least identify, for example, town locations, but that's not a summary. So summaries is one issue, and I think my friends are going to raise that. Translation. This morning's information is that the outstanding translation from B/C/S into English should be completed within a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which documents are those which are untranslated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From B/C/S into English, I'm afraid to say I haven't those details to hand, but they are statements and, I think, exhibits, I'm not sure, or attachments. As to translation the other way around, from English into B/C/S, subject to the other requirements of the Tribunal as a whole being given greater priority or being deemed to have greater priority by the department, the estimate was of one month for completion of that translation. It was proposed to me that we might prioritise with the translation unit material for translation, although to date I have not prioritised material for various reasons; it did not seem appropriate to do so. Subject to any other decisions that may be made today, I am, of course, prepared to ensure a sensible prioritisation of material. That, I think, leaves the additional witnesses today and the list that was served, together with the materials, in compliance with the order last Friday. One observation: The list is, of course, long, and it may well be longer than the Court or, indeed, the parties, at earlier stages, forecast. There are several reasons for that. First, the Prosecution does not know the Defence case at all and, within limits, has to allow for all possibilities. We know there is provision for rebuttal. We would rather, in the conventional way, take care of all identified issues as part of our case. Second, not only is there no knowledge of the Defence case, but despite efforts that have been made -- I make absolutely no complaint because those representing the defendants have to act on instructions, of course -- but on indications to date, agreement of facts may prove rather difficult. So far, very little, if anything material, has been capable of agreement. In those circumstances, we have to approach the case on the basis that everything will have to be proved, which means in relation to particular topics, it is essential at this stage that we identify all the witnesses who might prove a particular issue or topic, although with the unfolding of evidence, we have every expectation that there will be a very large number of them, the identified witnesses, who, of course, will not be called, even if -- it cannot be possible, for example, to have witness statements read, summarised, or agreed as we had all perhaps earlier hoped. Third, and really building on those first points, there has been a general encouragement from Mr. Smith to be, as it were, overinclusive -- I can't remember his precise term but he used it on the last occasion -- to overprovide, and indeed the Court's order by which we were required to provide statements last Friday underlined what may be the practice about adding to materials after today's date. So the list is long, but it is a great deal longer than it is, in reality, expected will be the number of witnesses called to give evidence. Can that bring me back to summaries and whether summaries or full statements are an appropriate way for the Court to proceed? Of course, there would be no expectation on our part of a Court, even if in principle it worked with full statements, being expected to go through this number of statements. If, in principle, the Court would prefer to have statements, there are various possible ways of proceeding. One is that the Court, like my learned friends, of course, will be notified a fortnight in advance of witnesses forthcoming, and that that would provide enough of a forecast or foreshadowing of evidence for the Court. If not, then an alternative route that I have considered this morning, although I haven't yet had a chance to discuss it with my own colleagues because they have all been busy on other things, but an alternative course would be that we could identify, within the overall lists of witnesses, core witnesses who we have every expectation of calling in any event, and those could be witnesses who the Court, if they so decided, would find it helpful to read, and it will be possible perhaps to summarise others. That's one possible solution to that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I realise there has been discussion through the usual channels. What the Rules require are summaries, and I think with this number of witnesses, we will require summaries. Let me, at the outset, make this plain: The number of witnesses, as you say, Mr. Nice, is far greater than anything that was forecast. A trial with 334 witnesses or anything approaching that is wholly unacceptable. It is an imposition on the Chamber, on the Court, it is an imposition on the Defence, and cannot be tolerated. The position is that this institution, this Tribunal, is in the position of the trials taking far longer than anybody had anticipated, with the result that men are in custody for a long time before their cases are brought to trial. All of this is a matter clearly of grave concern, and I say that at the outset so it can be heard, that this Chamber is proactive and we will take a view about, it may be, the overall number of witnesses which should be called. I remind you of Rule 73 bis (C) and (D) which permits the Trial Chamber to call upon the Prosecutor to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief for some witnesses and to reduce the number of witnesses if it considers that an excessive number of witnesses are being called to prove the same facts. The expression "call upon" is rather Delphic, and I think that we may be inclined to take a more active view of that. Clearly it is for the Prosecution to prosecute and not for the Trial Chamber to interfere with that right, but that said, it is for the Trial Chamber to control the proceedings, and that includes the amount of evidence that is put before it that is acceptable. Now, we hear what you say when you say that you do not intend to call or you don't anticipate that all or anything like that number of witnesses will be called. But what, from the outset, I would invite you to have in mind is that we will take a view, in due course, if matters are prolonged, about the number of witnesses who are to be called to prove a point, and if necessary, we will impose an order. So in those circumstances you may think it sensible to call your best witnesses as early as you can with a view to ensuring that those are heard. I understand in Blaskic that matters started off in much the same way, with the Prosecution producing or saying they're going to produce some 300 witnesses, and the Trial Chamber took a view about that. In the event, just over 100 were heard. That's a lot, but it's clearly a much more acceptable figure. The upshot is this: That I would invite you to have in mind the Trial Chamber's powers, and what I said, and the fact that we shall be exercising them. It's against that background that we will require summaries of these various witnesses. They need not be lengthy. If you wish to serve, if you think it right to serve the statements upon the Trial Chamber, so be it, but we will require summaries of them in order that we can understand the case fully and grasp what it is that is proposed that the witnesses should say. These need not be detailed; a reference to the village, or the issue is, and a very short summary of what it's proposed the witness would say would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will comply with that, of course. Indeed, before we left on hold the issue of what the Court would require, an exercise had been started. I should be able to comply with that requirement, I hope reasonably swiftly, although not immediately. It will take some time to accomplish that. As to the exercise by the Court of its powers, I have fully forecast that the Court would have those powers in mind and indeed would substantially want the Court to do so because, from the beginning, my concern and our concern has been to bring this case not only to trial, but to get through the trial swiftly. Can I just, however, first of all remind the Court that in its most recent order it underlined the fact that the further evidence requirements are limited, in the judgment of the Court, to new developments in investigation, which is one of the reasons we have to list witnesses at this stage. Can I simply remind the Court that the attitude of witnesses to coming to the Tribunal is changeable over time, and if, of course, witnesses of first choice are no longer available to us for whatever reason, we really have to have listed the witnesses who can help in that same area. So that's why there are so many witnesses listed. Can I return to that issue in just a minute, with a reference to one of the documents I'm proposing to help the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, before you do, let us deal with this matter of summaries. I anticipate it will form part of the order. When do you expect you can have the summaries ready, or the bulk of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The bulk of them, I would hope, in a few weeks. Not next week or the week after, I would think, only shortly before trial, but they can be provided on a rolling basis. Because in this case, if there are existing documents, that is, first-draft summaries, to work on, as those summaries are tidied up, they can simply be handed over in batches. It doesn't have to go through me on every occasion for a final decision because the document is not a document of record, it is a document of guidance and assistance. So it doesn't have to be brought for final decision and can be simply worked on by people and sent out. But I don't think completion could be effected, given all our other duties at the moment, either (a), by the time of the delivery of the pre-trial brief, which certainly will be occupying my time over the next ten days, as will other documentary exercises in which I'm going to be involved, so I think it can be provided by then in full, but we can easily provide a rolling series of summaries. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be sensible to look at it in this way: At least half the statements, at least half the summaries, I mean, by some date at the beginning of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- the remainder within three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure we could accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's just that it ought to be in an order. So the 6th of April I see is the date for the Defence pre-trial brief, so the 6th of April, half the summaries; the remainder three weeks later. Of course we come on to the question of the batting order of your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's been agreed, incidentally, with my learned friends yesterday at the meeting. I can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The summary is to include, clearly, those witnesses who are to be called first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was responding to Your Honour's earlier points. I don't know if I can just conclude what I was going to say about that. The Court refers to the large number of statements in its general observations. There is very limited prospect of agreement here, and it may be that practices as to agreement and admissions differ. It can be the case -- and I rather forecast this from some of the things that Mr. Smith said on earlier hearings -- that where facts are overwhelmingly proved by evidence to a common effect, and where there is no contrary case, then, typically, in some jurisdictions those matters can either be read or agreed because they're not actively challenged. Now, I don't know what, if anything, is the impediment to any agreement in this case, and it may, of course, be that agreements are in due course made. Typically, in some jurisdictions, one would discover what those impediments are in cross-examination because cross-examination will identify issues. I know cross-examination is another topic to which we must turn. Here, if cross-examination is of the form that I have proposed in our motion, then by one means or another, evidence will be shortened. Because of course, if matters aren't challenged, then it is possible, at a stroke, to excise a whole lot of evidence that would simply go to the same effect. Finally, I said I would mention one of the documents that I have served because it's a convenient time just to draw it to your attention and then make one other observation about an existing document. If the Court would be good enough to look at enclosure 2 of our recent motion -- or annex 2, I beg your pardon -- and to the third sheet in from the back, you will see one document that is in the process of preparation and will, in all probability, be completed in the same form by the time of the service of the pre-trial brief. Page 7, as you have it here, is a sample page. Page 7 at the bottom, that is. I beg your pardon; it's called Annex 3. I'm grateful to Ms. Verhaag. It's called Annex 3, and in my papers it's attached to Annex 2. Annex 3: What I've had done here is the following: The top part of the page sets out the count in the amended indictment. This is imprisonment and confinement of Muslims but with several identified locations. The dates are set out, the count numbers, the characteristics, and texts for the crime. Given that this amended indictment contains specified locations, I am obviously under a duty, within reason, to satisfy the test for each location. What follows is an identification, location by location, of which witnesses can give evidence on that topic for that location. Now, it had occurred to me, and it still does occur to me, that this document will be a useful document in any event, for the Court, as a working document. Without going to the longest one, if you go to the third entry, Vitez SDK offices, you can see that there are one, two, three -- four witnesses there who can support, at least it is forecast, can support that allegation. The Court will also see that by use of this document or something broadly similar, and by knowing at the stage that evidence is given where the matters are challenged, it will in fact be possible for us in a sensible, systematic, and workmanlike way to reduce very substantially the number of witnesses who will be called, provided only that we know what the issues are. The second thing that I can tell the Court -- I'm so sorry. If Your Honour didn't have it, I'll take a pause while he looks at it. I've said in my motion, or the motion, that this may be preferable, so far as the Court is concerned, to the requirement under 73 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So sorry. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we think this was a very helpful document because clearly it will spell out the various issues and who it is proposed to call upon them. Clearly you will have in mind calling your best witnesses, or the witnesses on whom you intend to rely most in each case, early on, and the rest will be purely corroborative of the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that there comes a time when the matter is established, or is established as far as it ever is going to be by the witnesses, and this will be helpful in determining that. Could I raise one other matter with you, a more general matter, while we are discussing this? It seems to me that there are two, or will be two, broad issues in the trial. The first broad issue is whether these crimes were committed at all. So taking the example we have in front of us, is it established that Muslims were confined and imprisoned in Kaonik prison? Now, that is essentially, is it not, by way of background, in the sense that it's proving that a crime was committed? The other broad issue, if we're satisfied as to the commission of a crime in a particular instance, is whether it is proved that these accused or either of them was in fact a participant in the crime. Now, it seems to me, thinking about these matters, that the first of those issues is one which one would hope there could be a broad agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As to whether the crimes were committed or not; if not broad agreement, that any issue as to whether the crime was committed could be limited, so that the time of the Trial Chamber is not taken up with essentially background issues, not, perhaps, concentrating on the crucial issues as to whether there has been any involvement proved by either of these accused. We would therefore encourage the parties, as far as possible, to agree on these background matters. It may be that both sides would have to compromise and a more neutral approach would have to be taken, but taking up a lot of time litigating in this particular trial, whether, for instance, there was imprisonment and confinement in the Kaonik prison, is one thing which we would not encourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I entirely agree with the expressions of views, insofar as they are, of the Chamber about the desirability of agreeing underlying facts. Before I part from this document, then, we will complete a document for all counts in the format of the document before you. This observation: In my recent motion, it may be inferred that I was proposing that this was an alternative to the requirement under 73(B)(c), that the list of witnesses should include the points in the indictment to which each witness will testify. Not so the witness list prepared for today's hearings -- I have a draft already, but the final version will come, I hope, before the end of the morning, or indeed before the break -- in fact identifies for all witnesses the counts to which that witness's evidence shall go, so that the Court will have the issue dealt with from both sides: Witness to points in the indictment, points in the indictment and witnesses; it has it each way round. Dealing with the -- no, just before I leave these witnesses, one other point: Yesterday, in the meeting, I can tell you Mr. Kovacic raised -- and I think, on reflection, very sensibly raised the issue of would we inform them if and when we knew that a witness is not going to feature because he's refused or for whatever other reason. Of course, sometimes an indicated refusal leads to a second inquiry, but there comes a time when you draw the line. It seems to me that that request by Mr. Kovacic is a sensible one, not least because there should be no representation of an ability to call evidence that you're not able to call by the conduct of a Prosecutor, at least in my judgment. Secondly, on a much more practical basis, if we can go through these lists one way or the other and strike names out, then the lists become even more useful. So I hope that will comfort Mr. Kovacic, but it seems a sensible proposal that he made. The other point I perhaps just ought to emphasise, for the Court's assistance, comes from Annex 1 of the motion, and I don't know if you've had an opportunity to look at that, but it's helpful to consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, except that the copy that I have, the second page is blank. So I haven't got the list of admissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry about that. What Your Honour should have is on the inside of the front page, the request, then a blank page, then something headed "Agreed Facts and Admissions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I hand mine in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- simply to save time, first of all, reminding myself of the order of things, and I'll look at somebody else's. If the Court hasn't had this as an annex, I'm very sorry. It was certainly filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is that we have got that, but where it is, I don't know. It doesn't appear in my documents as I have them at the moment. But don't worry, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are two documents there of significance or importance in the conduct of the case. First of all, there is the letter from Mr. Scott which reflected an earlier letter sent as long ago as November 1998, last year, requesting a range of admissions and as to which the Defence are only in a position to agree the first seven, and it may be that the Court would want to have a look at the issues that appear to be requiring determination from the remaining topics. Some of those, it would seem to us -- one has only to look at, I don't know, 12 or 15 -- I mean, many of them, it would seem should be capable of agreement, if not most of them, but, as I say, I make no complaint because if the defendants have given instructions that require all matters to be litigated, that is not something over which I have no control. But there are up to 37 admissions which Mr. Scott helpfully identified last year as being capable, he had hoped, of admission. We then turn to the next sheets, though you will find a letter dated the 28th of February from Sabine Bauer on my behalf to Mr. Turner Smith with a copy to Mr. Kovacic -- it's not a copy, a similar letter to Mr. Kovacic, I beg your pardon. The first document that appears there is a synthesis of the evidence given by an expert under cross-examination in the Blaskic trial. There had been, at an earlier stage, reference by Mr. Smith to the possibility of testimony in the earlier trials being read in full, and that is obviously a great deal better than causing a witness to come and say exactly the same thing a second time where everything that would be wanted of the witness has already been given, and it had seemed that this witness, for whatever reason, I may not be able to call live in these proceedings, has nevertheless given evidence of an expert nature, cross-examined on behalf of Blaskic, and that evidence might easily, it had been thought, be of value to this Tribunal. But rather than have it in full and rather labourious -- and that is offensive, unintentionally -- full examination and cross-examination, which is labourious to read, it seemed prudent for us to attempt the exercise reflecting Mr. Smith's earlier suggestion about the use of earlier testimony to synthesise the material, to get the witness to approve it in that state, and to offer it for agreement. But, unfortunately, that can't be agreed. If the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause there. Just pause there. Let us consider the summary of testimony given in Blaskic by Dr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It raises a broader question of principle which is how right is it to relitigate issues which have been litigated in Blaskic in this trial? Now, of course, I take the point that this is a separate case, these are different accused, and therefore, broadly, there is a right to cross-examine. But the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski decided that the transcripts of evidence in one case were admissible in another as hearsay evidence, and I would invite the parties to consider how far that can be used in this trial by way of expediting a hearing. Even if the full transcripts cannot be used, taking the case of this particular witness, to explore the possibility of using this statement which, if I may say so, is a much more digestible document than a transcript and much more helpful to a court, how far it would be possible to use this as evidence in chief and, if it was felt necessary to ask particular questions in this case, to have the witness here simply to be cross-examined and thereby save the time of all the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All of which I agree. In the case of this particular witness, as I have indicated, he may not be available to us live, but I raised with Mr. Smith, I think in correspondence -- better check that -- "If there are just one or two issues in addition to those already raised that you want to raise, why not ask whether he can agree those?" Of course, I have very much in mind the experience where -- from other jurisdictions where competing experts are invited to discuss matters together to produce a common report and where experts are much more freely available to the other side for discussion and so on than might be the practice here, but those other practices all lead to the better presentation to the trier of fact of expert opinions than slogging it out, in the vernacular, on both sides at great length. Any witnesses that can be read or agreed -- sorry, read from earlier cases or whose evidence can be summarised in this way or in some other way, we judge would be extremely helpful to this Chamber, but to some degree, if not almost wholly, we are now in the hands of the Defence subject to the reach of the ruling in the other case that has just been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that you would want to put in an application in relation to this particular witness, for instance, and any others in a similar position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then, of course, we would have to rule upon the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, you're referring to this annex and to the possibility, as the Presiding Judge just said, of having the transcript of this witness on the facts, Mr. Pajic. On the following page, 5.136, there is the opinion of the expert, and we have our own idea about the cross-examination, that is to say, that by looking at this document, we can see there are facts and there are the interpretations of those facts because we say that their creation was, for example, for defence reasons. "These amendments show the HZ-HB's aspiration to secede" and so on, "The Defence in cross-examination alleged 'that aggression from the Yugoslav Army and the Chetniks' and the impotence of the government in Sarajevo led the HZ-HB to organise themselves for the sole purpose of defence." It is my question then, don't you feel -- and perhaps this question also applies to the Defence -- that once we have examined the same facts, then we could distinguish between the facts themselves, which are indisputable and which exist and through different means, unless, of course, the Defence wishes to dispute this fact, and also the interpretation of the fact because at a given point in time, we can say that some of these facts are established facts, adjudicated facts. We can say, for example, that there were prisoner camps and there was an organisation for defence, there was a proclamation made by the republic, et cetera. So, in a way, there is also a way in which these facts are interpreted by one side or another and the meaning that may be given to these facts. If you are in agreement with the Defence, then we could perhaps avoid having to reprove facts which have already been proven and that no one intends to dispute, unless, of course, one wishes to dispute the facts themselves, in which case then we must go immediately to the meaning you would like to give to these facts, which could be different from one case to another. That is the question I would like to put to you, which also is addressed to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am certainly hopeful that underlying facts will emerge as agreed or, indeed, can be agreed from the beginning, and indeed the expert's opinion, where an expert is called, would more conveniently arise on agreed or established facts, for him to have to be postulating facts and suggesting conclusions in the event that those facts ultimately are proved. So, yes, indeed, it is highly desirable that facts can be agreed or, alternatively, proved or effectively proved by the time that the expert comes to give his evidence. The only other point I would make that derives from Your Honour's question is that you will see that this synthesis that I have produced takes into account cross-examination, and if we've missed something in the cross-examination that the Defence would want in, it is the sort of document that is capable by agreement of amendment for the better presentation to the Chamber. I don't know if that meets Judge Bennouna's concerns. If so, can I turn to the next document in the same annex? The Chamber will recall reference on the last hearing to something called a statement of facts. Now, I don't know if the Chamber has had an opportunity to read and consider that statement of facts. It is one of the annexes to this. In fact, it is Annex 2, and if the Chamber hasn't read it, it will find it an extremely useful summary of the case against these defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It was that that I had in mind when referring to the two broad issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because it contains, helpfully, the cases it has put against the individuals as it has put individual perpetrators and includes these two accused and then there are a number of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are some others identified. So the document is a very helpful summary of the Prosecution's case, and as the Court will realise, the Defence have had this document for a year. Contained within that document were analyses of the evidence on a village-by-village basis. A later document, served ex parte and discussed lightly at the last hearing, but served ex parte and with respect to the application to amend the indictment, contained a similar analysis village by village for other locations. If the Tribunal would turn now to what is page 5.129, there begins a document which is an extract absolutely word for word, no amendments of any kind, from those two documents: the statement of facts and the document served on Judge McDonald ex parte and part of a document that is not a public document, but it seemed to me that it would be helpful to serve on the Defence, for consideration for agreement, an analysis of the village-by-village evidence. Again, if we move to one that is shorter rather than longer, so if we turn over one sheet to 5.128, Behrici, paragraph 8 identifies simply the location, the census returns of the village; paragraph 9 sets out that the village was attacked by the HVO on the 18th of April -- the dates are set out separately on the left-hand column -- on this day there was only sporadic fire, shooting could be heard from the direction of Gomionica and Svinjarevo, and as a result, most of the people of Behrici fled on the 18th and the following days. About 40 or 50 men remained who were able to fight and so on. Now, I wrote to my learned friends inviting them not actually at that stage immediately to agree these facts but to give consideration to agreeing them. What I meant by that was explained in a later phone call dealt with by Mr. Scott initially, and it came to this: Of course, where you've got detailed facts, as set out here, in respect of villages for which other evidence has been given in other cases and for which some evidence may be given in this case in any event, there has to be some flexibility. Putting it shortly and giving a typical example, if an analysis of a village speaks of the village being defended by ten men and either evidence in another case or a witness makes it clear that it was 12, 15, or 20, whatever the Defence might have initially been prepared to agree has got to be subject to the potential for correction and some alteration. So I had in mind the realities of these cases. Nevertheless, it seems to me that it would save months of time if the underlying facts on a village-by-village basis could be agreed. Now, let's not beat about the bush. If all is agreed save HVO, we could be told that and we could focus our evidence on those bits of the evidence that go to show who the perpetrators were. That analysis, as Your Honours will see, covers all villages and locations. At the moment, as I understand it, the Defence are not able to agree any of this, and as I understand it, not even the geographical locations of the villages or the census returns detailing the composition of the villages, and that's unfortunate. It seems to us that this case would become immensely more manageable were we in the happy position of being able to agree the underlying facts subject to whatever reservations the Defence case may oblige them to make. Perhaps this brings me back to the distinction and approach to admissions that may exist in different jurisdictions. In the jurisdiction where, if you're presented with 20 statements on a topic on which you have no instructions, specific instructions to counter the statements, you can, quite responsibly, make the decision to agree them. Perhaps there are other jurisdictions which say you must never do any such thing; you must simply compel the prosecutor, in trench warfare, to move every part of his case inch by inch. Ultimately, if that's what's required of us, that's what we'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with something while it is in my mind. It really goes back to Rule 73 bis. I see that we are on 73 bis (ii). We have ordered a pre-trial brief, we have fixed a date for trial, and we are on admissions by the parties and a statement of contested matters of fact and law. It would be of immense assistance to the Trial Chamber to have agreement about matters which really cannot be a subject of dispute, such as the position of the village, the fact that there was a census, the fact that there was an attack and damage was caused and there were casualties. If there is agreement about such matters, then at least they don't have to be proved and the Trial Chamber can concentrate on the important things, which may be the nature of the attack and who was involved in it. Mr. Nice, this is a matter which does involve the Prosecutor, which is this: The way in which evidence is given varies, and in some jurisdictions, I think it's called the narrative form of giving of evidence is followed and the witness simply tells his or her story. Speaking for myself, I should say, and I underline that, that does take up a lot of time, in my view, and I would wish -- again speaking for myself; we will have to discuss it as a Trial Chamber -- but I hope that it will be possible in this case to have the witnesses concentrate on the important issues, and if matters can be got out of the way by way of agreement, then witnesses can give their evidence briefly and succinctly on the particular point in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Precisely so. I made some passing reference to this in the motion on procedure, proposing indeed that matters not in dispute be agreed and that the traditional form of direct examination, as the Americans call it, or examination-in-chief, as we know it, should be pursued. That indeed would save huge amounts of time, and if there was only one dispute as to a uniform or the material available to identify the nature of an attacking person, although I'm still not suggesting anything like the number of witnesses listed all together would be called, but, in fact, you can get through a large number of issues in a short space of time when the issues are narrowed in that way. Can I, rather than keep popping up and down, since I have been dealing with the possibility for agreement, deal with one other document now? It's Annex 4, I think. It was something that we discussed at the meeting of counsel yesterday. I trust the Court has the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Annex 4. Again, I understand that practices on either side of the Atlantic differ, and it may well be that it would be thought I am being far too generous to the defendants in proposing the preparation and service of a document of this kind by those more familiar with the American practice, and it may be that in America, documents of this kind are reserved for service until the end of the trial at the earliest, in the same way, as I understand, that exhibits aren't shown in opening statements in detail, apparently, but still ... I am afraid to say I have to be guided by my own experience of what is likely to help a Trial Chamber, and it seemed to me, in a case that has a wide geographical sweep and a wide sweep of time, that the Chamber will want some kind of route map through the materials of one kind or another. The best route map, in my experience, is a chronology that draws together either all or nearly all of the different types of material. So here you have -- and it's in draft only -- simply two sheets and a bit of what I am prepared to make available to the Chamber and, of course, to my learned friends. You can see exactly how things are set out: date, place, where relevant, and event, and then a column permitting the Defence to admit or to make other comment as to the fact, an exhibit, where the exhibit is material, and a column indicating whether the exhibit is admitted for what it is. If we just run through the first few entries, the first entry, recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the European Community and, similarly, by the United States, something about the presidency of HZ-HB, then in italics, because it concerns Cerkez more than Kordic, a meeting between Muslims, and names are identified, and so on, in Vitez; then another reference to a crisis meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt, if I may, just to understand something. What is the purpose of italics?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Italics distinguishes material specific to Cerkez from material specific to Kordic. Then we come to, on the 22nd of April, an order from Kordic issued under the authority of the Ministry of Defence with the order number given, that is, the institution's identifying marks given; 3rd of May, in Busovaca, a decision by HZ-HB signed by Kordic, and so on. A schedule of this form, apart from providing the Chamber with a route map through the material, would place the Defence in the ideal position of being able to mark what is agreed and what is challenged. Now, documented meetings of the defendants, documented by their own documents, frankly should not be challenged. This isn't a game. It is not a "Can you prove the document, and if you prove the document, we will reluctantly not challenge it"; this is a trial on an important issue, and there have been protestations about the willingness to agree matters. Now, I have tried it two ways. I have always indicated this document was coming, as the Court will remember, from the end of last year, the very first hearing I think I mentioned it. So this document has always been in my mind, and I also tried it the other way with the document that summarises the position on a village-by-village basis, and Mr. Scott has made his attempt with the letter of November 1998. I understand that my learned friends have some reservations about even receiving this document, let alone responding to it, I may be wrong, but that is as I understand the position. I remain willing to complete the preparation of this document, and as I have said in my motion, it is a document that doesn't have to stop, doesn't have to be frozen at the time of the opening of the case because with comparatively limited but sensible, disciplined measures, the document can be updated from time to time in response to what elements, for example, the Chamber might itself want included on it, and then reprinted and recirculated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, it is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is not evidence and it is not a substitute for evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can only be for assistance and guidance, and, of course, there is no reason why the Defence should not write upon it themselves --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to add whatever it is they wanted to add and, of course, as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, it would be of assistance merely in following the evidence. Matters which are not proved can simply be crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I may mention what will be a common refrain, which is that we are not a jury. We are experienced in dealing with these matters. If a matter is not proved, we will simply cross it out and forget it. There is no difficulty about that. I would like that to be heard so that it may be understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's that proposal, and I will respond at the end of today's hearing and in the following week to whatever is the Chamber's decision about what would help it. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, we will hear you, of course, about all these matters. We are not going to rule. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have merely taken a preliminary view about this, and I say it so the Defence can hear, that our preliminary view is to encourage this kind of endeavour because it makes the trial much easier to manage for us. It proves nothing, but it does indicate what the issues are, and in due course, we would encourage the Defence to produce a similar document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or indeed to make entries on ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly to comment on your document, that would be very helpful, and if need be, to incorporate their own material into the document so it becomes a common document. I might say this, that in my experience of cases -- not criminal cases but other cases, commercial cases, family cases even, where you have a long history of disputed matters of fact and sometimes complex matters of fact over a marriage or a commercial dispute or something like that, it is extremely helpful to have a chronology as being a particular format, one way in which the material can be approached, and it is very helpful to have both sides to put their account of the matter in the chronology. We will leave that for the moment and hear what the Defence have to say. Is there anything else you want to say about --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. The only other point connected to the matters I have recently been discussing is that, of course, another way in which we may get agreement is under 73(F), the Defence pre-trial statement, and, of course, they can be required there to give a statement admitting facts and law, facts within the power of the Chamber, and I, of course, leave it entirely to you to decide how, if at all, to use that power to establish what is truly in dispute. That concludes what I say in answer to what was the initial question, are we basically in compliance. Subject to the reservations that I have made and the additional witnesses, which list will be served when it is properly printed, yes, we believe we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And are you ready for trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, in the pre-trial motion you filed on the 25th of March, in Rule 73 bis, there is also a logic that must be followed. There is a matter, of course, as you said, that treats matters of facts and law, and there is also -- whether the term should be pre-defence conference for the same matters. We need to find whether or not there is a common denominator, but in matters of law, there is no common denominator. There is a framework in which people can meet and where there will be divergent points. What you have proposed as a document as far as procedure is concerned, which I see there is also a statement of law as well, I wonder whether or not you are going to present to us on the 25th of March this matter as well, because if you are going to do so, then we need not double or overlap your efforts. Perhaps on the 25th of March you can file a document as complete as possible in which you would describe what occurred, the basis of the Prosecution and all the related events, and then the way in which you intend to analyse those events in order to give us a very clear idea of the prosecution, what happened, and why the accused are personally implicated in those events, and then a response will be submitted. This is provided for by the Rules. And then, at a moment in time, as the Presiding Judge has just stated, since we are supposed to be professionals and knowledgeable in this area, we will then determine on our own what are disputed or not disputed, and then we will try to see whether or not there is an admission by both parties, and then we may address both parties on this issue. Can you please respond to this question: First of all, this brief that we are expecting from you, will it include elements which we already have before us now? In this case, then I would encourage you quite simply to submit as clear a brief as possible and as complete as possible, including the tables, including the tables on the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was no misunderstanding by me as to whether the schedule I propose could substitute for the pre-trial brief. It can't. The pre-trial brief, which will deal with matters of fact and law, will be a freestanding document. The chronology will come as an attachment, I suppose, to it, or simply with it. So the Court will have both types of document. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the position is that you are in a position to serve with the pre-trial brief any schedules on which you intend to rely -- or, rather, a chronology and a schedule related to the indictment, and I have in mind your documents Annex 3 and 4. They will be served --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They will be served as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we ordered that, it may be that we can order a response to it too, if we were to order it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you were so to decide, we would have no objection because it is my settled intention, subject to your indicating otherwise, that those documents will be prepared and made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it may be convenient now to move to the Defence. It is getting on for break time. I have in mind that we have still to consider the various orders which the Prosecution have asked for in their latest motion, but it may be convenient after the break to hear the Defence on what has been discussed so far. I will have distributed a proposed calendar and proposed sitting times. We have drawn up a schedule which is intended to go through till the recess at the beginning of August. Before you see it, I should tell you that we intend sitting most but not all weeks in this trial. There are two matters to be borne in mind: Some of the sitting days will be half days. That is necessitated because I am in another Trial Chamber conducting another trial on the mornings of those particular weeks, so that is why there are half weeks. The other matter is that, of course, this is not the only case which this Trial Chamber has on its list, and accordingly, there will be breaks when other cases will have to be heard. Anybody wanting to make any submissions about the calendar, of course, is free to do so. We have included proposed sitting times which we hope will accommodate counsel and also all those who are involved in the trial, the technical staff, the interpreters, and everybody else. But we hope we have managed to accommodate all those interests. I will have that distributed and then we will discuss it in due course. Yes. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the Defence. Mr. Smith? If you would like to get through those matters which you wish to raise with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had in mind responding on all of the issues that have been addressed to date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- not responding at this point on the procedural issues raised in the Prosecutor's latest motion or on the release question, judging those to be for the next portion of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like to start out distinguishing, as this Court did in its February 26th order, between Rule 66(A)(ii) and the requirement for production of statements -- the discovery obligation, on the one hand, and the 73 bis (B)(iv) obligation for the production of a witness list and the other listed matters under 73 bis (B)(iv) -- and note that in Your Honour's order, you've indicated, and I think indicated by starting out this morning to address each separately. I quote from your order that "The obligation to disclose witness statements to the Defence under Rule 66(A)(i) is independent of and does not rely upon finalisation of ..." and then the matters relating to witness lists. On the question of statements, I'm going to pick up several points from the discussion and then move to 73 bis (B)(iv) first and then the discovery issue second. It is true that the defendants have argued ever since we filed our motion to compel, back in July, for more rather than less and sooner rather than later. That is to say, we urged the Prosecutor, in the production of witness statements, to be overinclusive, and we did so with the thought in mind that if done early, when the Defence can cope with the overinclusive approach, it would aid in both the preparation of the Defence and aid the Prosecutor by sequential production, as Your Honours have referred to in your own order of February 26th. And if we were given access to the prior statements in the form of transcripts and exhibits from other cases, it would also aid the Defence in attempting to help the Court and the Prosecution structure this very broad and very difficult case that the Prosecution has pled. I might draw Your Honour's attention to the language in our original notice of motion to allow access to non-public materials, where we cited Judge Jorda's desire, articulated as early as the spring, before we were involved in this case, when Mr. Naumovski was just the counsel, for innovative techniques. We indicated that we were prepared to do that, but that without access to the necessary material so that we played with a full deck of cards in assessing the truth of facts and the availability of witnesses and testimony, it would be very difficult for the parties on either side to comply with the request for innovative techniques, but most difficult for the Defence because, of course, the Prosecution, being a unitary prosecutor, has had all along, for over four years, access to all of the materials that they were both producing to bring the case against these defendants, and that they have been using year after year in these existing ongoing proceedings on the Lasva Valley. We indicated at the outset, in a motion for access to non-public materials, that the volume of material in this case was very significant, and just as we saw the supporting material at that time, before we got the additional supporting material, or at least some of it, from the amended indictment, much less the material from these other cases that is relevant. In our motion for access in July -- in our reply, rather, to the Prosecutor's motion -- we also argued that in the absence of timely disclosure of materials in discovery, there is little chance that the parties will be able to reach agreement as to these innovations. So I suggest to Your Honours that the Prosecutor comes late to the notion of techniques for structuring trial; that we have been arguing from the outset that the case needs to be structured in a way that allows us to assist the Trial Chamber in how to try the case. I would note that the Prosecutor argues that they do not know the Defence's case at this point and that that leaves them in some difficulty. But as Your Honours are fully aware, it is the Prosecutor that has the burden of proving the case it has chosen to plead beyond a reasonable doubt on every count, and given the number of villages in each count as to each such village. We have protested that method of proceeding, but we have been overruled. Nonetheless, it is the Prosecutor's burden to prove his case as he has pled it, and that case does not turn on the Defence's case. If he fails to plead his case and prove it in his case, he will be met by a motion to dismiss at the end of his case, before the Defence has even begun to put on its case. So I suggest to you that the position the Defence is going to take is a red herring on the question of what the Prosecutor has to do. They know perfectly well. They have pled a case, and they must prove it. Now, to the extent that we can assist the Trial Chamber in techniques relating to shortening the trial, we have said, as I indicated right from the outset, that we intend to do this, but, ultimately, it is not fair for the Prosecutor to be allowed to throw its burden of proving the case it has pled back on the defendant. As to -- and I will come back to this in a moment, but just a short aside on the proposed stipulations that have been filed on us by the Prosecution. In both cases, as Your Honours will have seen, these proposed stipulations are taken either verbatim or essentially paraphrased from the proposed statement of facts in the Prosecutor's supporting material. The proposed statement of facts is the case pled as an advocate by the Prosecution to persuade the confirming judge that the defendant is guilty. It should come as no surprise to the Prosecution that the Defence can't simply sign up to the Prosecutor's characterisation of the facts. Where there were simple facts, clearly stated, we have agreed, and we are prepared to continue doing that in the future, but when presented with a long series of proposed stipulations that are in effect the Prosecutor's case against our client, and then asked to agree, particularly as to the second set, when it is only given to us several weeks ago -- and as I will come in a moment, we are then inundated with additional material that we should have had long ere this. Seven months ago, nine months ago -- it is no wonder that our initial response is we will agree objective facts where we can, but separating the objective facts from the characterisations in your brief on the facts would take some time. Let me turn then to the question of summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt to say this: That clearly we appreciate, as a Trial Chamber, that there has been a volume of material which has been disclosed that you are having to cope with, and that any orders we make will be made with that fact in mind. Clearly we would not expect you to agree to anything which is in the nature of an interpretation of the facts, or a Prosecution case, or the way that they invite the Chamber to look at the facts, but what we would encourage you to do is to agree the facts, where that is possible, not the interpretation. But clearly you must have time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, thank you. We take that on board, and I might add that we have at no time said that we would be unwilling or unable to agree to the location of a particular village or what the 1991 census may say, but I will come back to that, and we will be as helpful as we can, as quickly as we can. Let me turn for a moment to the summaries, and there, I think, it will be of great help both to the Trial Chamber and the Defence to have summaries, and the Defence fully intends to produce such summaries when its part of the case is ready to be presented. I might suggest, in addition to the agreement, for the progress of the trial as a whole, of two weeks' standing notice of the specific witnesses and the order within the following two weeks, that particularly given the flood of material at this time, the Prosecution might agree to several things. First, an initial determination of the witnesses that it plans to call, say, in the first six weeks, so that the Trial Chamber has some sense of the initial flow of the schedule; and secondly -- and this is a point related to the distinction between a witness statement on the one hand and a witness list on the other. The witness list requirement of 17 bis (B)(iv) requires that the statements be of the witnesses the Prosecution intends to call. The Defence at this point is looking for a needle in a haystack in terms of the witnesses the Prosecution will really call, an obligation to give us a sense of the first six weeks' order, and which witnesses, would be very helpful. There are several other things that would be helpful. The Prosecution has proposed for every count to come up with a list of the key witnesses, and I think that is a useful document. I might propose that there the Prosecution simply flag the core witnesses so that both the Trial Chamber and the Defence know where to start and which witnesses are likely not to be called because they are only supplemental witnesses. Further, I think it would serve the Trial Chamber quite well, and be of help to the Defence, if the Prosecution did not give us a specific batting order for the entire trial, but rather were prepared to say how they're going about the proof. Are they going to start with experts and general background? Will they then start in Vitez, and march down the valley to Ahmici, and then Kaonik, and then Busovaca, and then Kiseljak? Will they start at the other end and come the other way back up? I'm certain that they must -- while they don't know it in detail at this time, they certainly have taken decisions about the basic way in which the case will be presented, and that could, I think, be very helpful in giving the Trial Chamber a sense of the overall structure of the way the trial will proceed, and will also be very helpful to the Defence in giving us an overall sense of where things start and where things end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to move from there, Mr. Smith, it may be helpful to have a reaction from the Prosecution on those suggestions, which seem to me, to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no problems with any of those suggestions. We agreed yesterday that the general rule for notification of witnesses -- which was what my learned friend asked for, and I was only too happy to agree -- should be, in general, two weeks, and that on any Friday, notification is given for the witnesses on the following Monday week, so that the minimum time that any one has -- and this would be mutual to both sides, the same for the Defence as the Prosecution -- the minimum that people have is one week and two weekends notification of witnesses to be called. That's the way it operates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will incorporate that in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. As to the first six weeks, subject to any problems about availability of particular witnesses, I hadn't been asked about that before, but if I had been, I would have said yes to that. As to a general plan of how I will present the evidence, I would have given that in any event, and I'm only too happy to undertake to do so. Again, it has to be subject to the necessary interpolation of witnesses who aren't available at other times, and so on and so forth, but in general, I'm only too happy to oblige.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter was flagging the core witnesses in each case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'd offered that at an earlier stage, as a solution to another problem, but I don't see any particular objection to flagging core witnesses for everyone's assistance. It seems quite a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and like my colleagues, I think that will aid in the presentation of the case. I would turn now to discovery, and I have dealt with Rule 73 bis (B)(iv) to the extent that I am going to at this point. It is the Defence's position, Your Honour, that the Prosecutor is not in fact in compliance with Rule 66 and its discovery requirements, and in fact it is in very substantial non-compliance. Let me start with the supporting material. We have just been served, on the 5th of March, with two new sets of materials said to be part of the supporting materials, and as Your Honours will recall, the supporting materials were to have been served by November 13th of 1998. It appears that -- well, one of these packages appears to have 54 documents; another 24 documents. We are still trying to process them, and it is not clear to us whether we are being served now with B/C/S translations of things we already have in English or whether these are new materials. There are a large number of witness statements in these materials, but they are specifically labelled, in the receipt that we're asked to sign, as part of the supporting materials. I would submit that they are late. I would further ask my learned colleague whether they know the status of the translation into B/C/S of the supporting materials that we have been furnished. Have we now got everything that has been translated? Is there, to your knowledge, still material left from last November that's to be translated? I say that, Your Honours, with the following thought in mind: Translation into B/C/S is by no means a technicality. It goes to the absolute heart of the defendant's ability to defend himself. The volume of materials in this case (amplification cutoff) does not speak or read English with any facility. He needs to be able to read the materials and to aid in the preparation of his defence. The B/C/S versions are absolutely essential in addition to being clearly called for by Rule 66(A), and clearly called for since last July. I don't know whether -- if you don't know the status, that's fine; we can chat about it later. But in short, we're not sure why we're still receiving supporting material at this late date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any other point on the discovery? And I call on Mr. Nice to hear of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour, but not on the supporting material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you went on, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- we'll deal with all the discovery points together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me turn, then, to the question of witness statements under 66(A)(ii). Here I think it is important to simply recall the language in Your Honour's February 26 order about the purpose and importance of the witness-statement requirement in Rule 66(A)(ii). I quote: "The obligation to provide witness statements pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) is intended to assist the Defence in the understanding of the case against the accused in accordance with his rights under Article 21 of the Statute, and should thus be provided to the Defence as far in advance of the trial as is possible, even if this means that statements are disclosed sequentially, and that statements are disclosed of witnesses who eventually are not called to testify in the matter." Indeed, Your Honour, we have argued, as you will know, that we have a right under Rule 6(C) and under the provisions of Rule 66, in effect at the time the indictment was issued, and the case became pending, to a service of all of the witness statements as soon as practicable, notwithstanding the fact that the rule was subsequently changed to say "at least not later than 60 days before trial," and then subsequently, "as the Court may direct." Now, I need to give Your Honours a sense of the position that the Defence has just been put in by the Prosecution. We have received a list as of March 5th and documents in boxes in our offices this week of 807 documents. Of those, roughly 240 are by the Prosecutor's own count previously disclosed. That means that we are now just within 30 days of trial, being given, under Rule 66(A)(ii), 570, give or take a few, brand new documents. In short, the Prosecution has just given us over twice as many new documents as the list they have previously given us under Rule 66. Secondly, if you look at the question of how many are translated into which languages -- a point, as I just indicated, that is absolutely fundamental to the adequate preparation of the Defence -- 267 of the English documents have not been translated into B/C/S. I must say it seems to me -- I will be delighted if the translation service can turn 267 documents around in one month, going from English to B/C/S, but I suspect that is a tall order. Secondly, there are, by our count, roughly 77 B/C/S documents not yet translated into English. Even turning those around in a fortnight may prove difficult. Finally, there are 32 miscellaneous documents that are neither in the language -- one of the official languages of the Tribunal nor in B/C/S. Those have got to be translated. In short, there are more yet to be translated than have been listed by the Prosecution -- the total being 376, plus or minus -- more yet to be translated than the Prosecution has indicated in this document were already served on the Defence, which are 240, plus or minus. Let me now look at these documents from the point of view of the number of witnesses involved. The original document given to us last Friday listed 334 total witnesses the Prosecutor intends to call, with the caveat, of course, that that's not really what he intends to call, but that's overinclusive. Of those, 54 witnesses are presented with no statements at this stage. 141, by our count, plus or minus, are new witnesses we were not aware of previously. 139, by our count, give or take some, and with redactions and pseudonyms it's difficult to be very precise, are previously disclosed witnesses. Now, Your Honours, I think, have fairly assessed the implications of the magnitude of this many witnesses for the trial as a whole, as you will know, in the Blaskic case, the Prosecutor called 102 witnesses, and the Defence has, I think, called at least 40 by now, and that case has gone on essentially two years. If you multiply out the number of witnesses, even if, let's say, the Prosecution drops 50 witnesses and you start with 300, and even if you assume one witness a day, which, given the track record in other cases, is extremely generous, you are still looking at 300 trial days, or roughly 60 trial weeks, and that's the Prosecution case alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, let me interrupt you on that. I've already made plain that the Trial Chamber will be proactive in controlling the number of witnesses. These are matters which we have in the forefront of our consideration. We also bear in mind that this case is now an old case, an old case, because the indictment was issued over three years ago; the two accused made their initial appearance as long ago as October 1997. To see this amount of material appearing at the last minute is a matter for grave concern, but perhaps you would like to tell us what you want us to do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will come to that, and might I simply note, in doing that, the last statistic that you may want to consider: In counting the documents, plus or minus, provided by this list with 334 -- and which they've now supplemented by another set of witnesses -- we find 22 statements dated in 1999, from which none have been translated yet. These are the most recent and one might have expected that they perhaps wouldn't be translated yet. 73 from 1998, only 3 of which have been translated. Everything else has been in the Prosecutor's possession from a date before 1998. I submit that the bulk of the material could and should have been disclosed either back in October of '97 or in October of '98, sequentially and overinclusive as we requested. But to do it now, in an overinclusive way, dramatically prejudices the Defence. Now, in terms of what we request Your Honours to do: The first request is -- and I think it's important to focus on the Rules. It is our position that there are violations here of the Tribunal's Rules and there are violations of this Trial Chamber's orders. Rule 37(A) of the Tribunal's Rules imposes on the Prosecutor a duty to obey the Rules of the Tribunal. Rule 5(A) of the Rules, which deals with non-compliance with the Rules, states that "Where an objection on the ground of non-compliance ... is raised by a party at the earliest opportunity," and I submit to you that as to the material just provided, this is the earliest opportunity, and indeed we have been trying to provide against this eventuality since we originally filed our motions for access and motions to compel -- but when an objection is raised "... at the earliest opportunity, the Trial Chamber shall grant relief if it finds that the alleged non-compliance is proved and that it has caused material prejudice to that party." You will note the distinction between Rule 5(A) and Rule 5(B). Rule 5(B) says that "Where such an objection is raised otherwise than at the earliest opportunity, the Trial Chamber may, in its discretion, grant relief." The relief we request, Your Honour, is as follows: First, we believe that the Trial Chamber should exclude all witnesses as to whom witness statements were served on or about March 5th up to the present, due first to a violation of the "as soon as practicable" requirements of Rule 66(A)(ii), and due secondly, to an abuse of the Trial Chamber's own order dated February 26th which gave the Prosecutor until March the 5th to finish up with his witness statements, but I would argue did not contemplate -- we certainly did not contemplate and were quite surprised at the extremely large number that have been served at the last minute under that allowance of the order, and which could have been served much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I seem to recollect that we gave the Prosecutor an extension of time, so effectively, we ruled on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed. And I should -- you have given them an extension until today, and I should have phrased it "the March 5 deadline as extended until today." Secondly, we believe that the Trial Chamber, in order to ensure a fair trial for the Defence -- that's the basis of the first requested relief -- should exclude all Prosecution witnesses on their list of 334 witnesses as to whom witness statements have yet to exist as of today and have yet to be served as of today either because they have not been properly translated -- as Your Honours will know, Rule 66 requires that they be served in Serbo-Croatian and I believe that it is Rule 3 that requires them to be served in a language of the Tribunal, so whether it is translating into English or translating into Serbo-Croatian, I believe that there is a violation of the Rules; and indeed, it seems to me, Your Honours, it can be argued that the transcripts of both the public hearings and the non-public hearings, which have been ruled by the Tribunal to be witness statements under Rule 66(A)(ii), are also owed to the defendant in his own language. Third, we would request that all of the material that should have been served be served forthwith, particularly -- I point Your Honour to the status of the materials from other Lasva Valley cases. We have now been given the public transcripts up through December from the Lasva Valley cases but only as of this week.
