utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is not a Rule, though, which deals with what the subject matter of cross-examination should be. It is a restrictive Rule, if I can put it that way, but it's not a prescriptive Rule which the Prosecution are seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's a very excellent point, Judge May, but if the Court wanted to adopt a prescriptive Rule as opposed to a restrictive Rule, it certainly knew how to do that in a general way, and it has not done that; and furthermore, I would point out that the Rule which is advocated by the Prosecution today is a Rule that has had no application in any of the Lasva Valley cases so far. It's not been applied in the Kupreskic case, it was not applied in the Furundzija case, it has absolutely not been applied in the Blaskic case, and it has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, it was applied in one case because I can remember instructing counsel to put their case on a particular issue whether -- I can't remember what the issue was -- but whether somebody was there or not, I think was the point. It doesn't matter. What is there to prevent counsel putting their case to the witness so that the witness has the opportunity, as it were, of answering? Suppose the example I give, if your case is that your client is not there when a particular incident happened and the witness says that he was, should you not put that to the witness so the witness has a chance of dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, to answer that question, Your Honour, I think that it might be useful, actually, to take a look at the derivation for the Rule that is explained in the authorities that were pointed out by the Prosecutor in its brief. The seminal case, I believe, is the English case of Browne v. Dunn. That was a libel case, a civil libel case, that was decided in 1894. It, of course, involved a jury trial context. The two opinions in that case that I would like to draw the Court's attention to I think address Your Honour's question in a very direct way. Lord Herschell's opinion in that case is -- he explained, in the course of writing for the majority, I believe, articulating the rule or the recommendation that the case be put to the witness in cross-examination. Lord Hershell, even during the course of the opinion explaining the rationale for that rule, stated: "Of course, I do not deny for a moment that there are cases where notice has been so distinctly and unmistakeably given and the point upon which he is impeached" -- the witness, that is -- "or is to be impeached is so manifest that it is not necessary to waste time putting questions to him upon it." So in the very case that articulates the rule -- and I will address in just a second the consequences of an inadvertent violation of that rule, if I may? -- but the very case that articulates the rule basically --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- exception to it. The second opinion comes from Lord Halsbury, and in that opinion, Lord Halsbury says: "I can quite understand a case in which a story told by a witness may have been so incredible and romancing a character --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request that the speaker slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: "... may be to ask him to leave the box. I therefore wish it to be understood that I would not concur in ruling that it was necessary in order to impeach a witness's credit that you should take him through the story which he has told --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: More requests for slowing down, Mr. Sayers, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- particularly if you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Anyway, Lord Halsbury made the point that: "I would not concur in ruling that it was necessary, in order to impeach a witness's credit, that you should take him through his story again which he had told giving him notice by the questions that you impeached his credit." I think the problem with the Prosecution's suggestion really comes with an inquiry as to what the consequences might be of advertently or inadvertently running afoul of the rule. Even in England, as far as I can ascertain, the cases are not clear. What is the level of detail that is required in order to put the case to the accused? Is minute detail required or just general detail? Once again, the cases are on both sides of that issue. Another good example is: What happens if you don't put the case to a chap who is obviously telling a tall story, a romancing story, to use Lord Halsbury's vivid phrase? Again, the cases are split. Some cases hold that this results in a concrete and irretrievable acceptance of the witness's testimony. Other cases, like O'Connell v. Adams, state that Justices have no duty to accept evidence merely because a witness is not challenged. Is the failure to cross-examine a witness on a particular point brought out in direct examination, does that result in a preclusion of the right to introduce evidence on that point? It could in some cases indicate, yes, that is the rule. Other cases, however, do not in the English system, a good example being O'Dogherty v. Gallagher that was decided four years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the counsel please slow down again for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, the decision is in the discretion of the trial judge and, frankly, we don't need that particular rule because you already have that discretion in Rule 90(G). Perhaps the most vivid demonstration of why there is wisdom in Rule 89(A) which states that the Trial Chamber is not to adopt national rules of evidence comes from the scholarly commentary on Browne v. Dunn, and I don't purport to be any expert upon this particular rule of cross-examination but I would point out to the Court that six years ago, one scholar named Gilles Renaud published an article in The Advocate which examined all of the underpinnings of the rule, its applications, cases in which it had been applied to exclude evidence, cases reaching a contrary result, and the title of the article was, "Case Comment: Regina v. MacKinnon: Has the Rule Requiring Notice of Future Impeachment been Un-Dunn?" A somewhat laboured pun but nonetheless a point that was rather well made, and the scholar actually makes this observation, Your Honours: "There is considerable doubt as to precisely when the rule is breached and also as to the penalties that attach to a party who is in breach of it; hence, can any rule be said to exist under these circumstances?" Yet, Your Honours, that's the rule that the Prosecution would seek to foist upon the Defence in this case. We do not think, and we vehemently oppose the imposition of any national rule of evidence that might apply in the courts of England or Wales to the proceedings before this Tribunal. There is no jury present in this Tribunal, as the Court has already observed today. So one of the reasons for that particular rule may not come into play at all during the course of cross-examination in this case. But more importantly, there is no rule that requires it, and indeed, there is a rule that deals expressly with cross-examination, Rule 90(H), albeit in a restrictive capacity and not prescriptive, as you say, but Rule 90(H) does not say what the Prosecutor now wishes it did say. Sometimes, Your Honours, we would submit, just as did Lord Halsbury and Lord Herschell, that sometimes the wisest cross-examination and the most prudent and most professional cross-examination may not be to cross-examine at all, but by having unclear and unfamiliar and rather hazy national rules apply that are fraught with pitfalls for the unwary, not familiar with the twists and turns of the jurisprudence that gave rise to that rule, we think is not consistent or consonant with the provisions of Rule 89(A) or 90(H) and for those reasons we oppose the application made by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sayers. Mr. Kovacic, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Mr. President, and Your Honours. I will be very brief. I would just like to add several things. If we go point by point from the Prosecution motion regarding examination-in-chief, we agree with my colleague at the bench. We have no objections. Regarding (b) and (c), I again completely support the arguments put forth by the Kordic Defence, and I would like to add the following in point (a), which is whether contact between the witness and counsel will be allowed after the oath has been taken. The rules have not spelled out details, and we think that the choice should be taken into account; at least absent rules, we feel that we need to have freedom of choice. Let me give you the local practice of the Republic of Croatia. The Criminal Code, Article 339 provides full freedom to the accused, and this is referring only to the situation where the accused is witness in his own case. He has the right during the examination-in-chief to consult with his counsel, but he cannot confer with him regarding the already-asked questions. So this is what I can refer you to with respect to the local jurisdiction. So the accused has the right to consult with his counsel, even in the days while he is testifying, but he cannot consult him with respect to the specific question once it is asked. So this is all I have to add with respect to Point A. Now, with respect to Point B, which addresses the time, that is, the order of Defence witnesses, let me again point out that the Rules have not been very specific in that regard. We need interpretations of the Rule in that respect. Let me first ask, what is the right of the Defence to decide, after the Prosecution case has been made, to proceed with the Defence on a particular issue or not? If the Defence considers that no proof has been presented by the Prosecution, it may choose not to present any evidence of its own. Also the Defence should have the right to make a decision whether its client will testify at any point during the presentation of evidence. We believe that the right of the defendant would be violated if it were to be forced to reach this decision ahead of time. I think that it should be based on the evidence presented by the Prosecution; it has to be able to see what the results are of its own evidence, what the full effect was, and then decide whether it is necessary or not to put its client on the witness stand. I think we also have to consider all the authorities. We have now quoted the British and U.S. sources; let me just also mention the local laws in Croatia. First of all, the old laws which were in force in all of the former Yugoslavia, we had a Criminal Code which was inquisitory. The old law that was in force in Croatia during the former Yugoslavia required that the trial began after the indictment was read, that the accused testified at first or used the right of silence. And if he choses not to use the right to testify, he could still, at any point during the trial, decide to testify, which meant that he could do it either during the trial or at the end of the trial. A new Criminal Code has now been adopted in Croatia, and in this new law, the approach has changed. In the new law, the new law provides that the accused -- and this is Article 334,2 -- that after the presentation of evidence, that is, after the case in chief has been concluded, the accused can testify. In other words, it is the position that has been adopted by the Defence here. In other words, he can testify at the end of the presentation of evidence. And I just want to add that the procedure in Croatian law does not distinguish between the Prosecution case in chief and the Defence case in chief; it is one procedure. My point is that if the rules did not go so far as to spell all details, we believe that this Chamber needs to follow certain universal legal principles and adopt such solution which would give the parties equality of arms and take into account fairness and justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to ask you a question about cross-examination, Mr. Kovacic. With regards to what Mr. Kovacic stated, the rules, Rule 90(B), which was cited a moment ago, states that, "In cases not otherwise provided for in this section, a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which best favour a fair determination of the matter before it, and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law." Therefore, now we're looking at the general context of the testimony, and the purpose here is to ensure that we have maintained balance and fairness. Of course, we must take into account national laws; these are principles which are generally drawn from national laws, in light, of course, of the Statute and of the Rules, and of course this is in accordance with our own Statute. But this is what this brings us to now. With regards to the cross-examination, there is a general principle, with regards to silence, that silence is interpreted depending on the context; it depends when that silence occurs. It all depends on the context in which the silence takes place when there is silence. There is an entire international jurisprudence on the subject; I will not invoke them here now. What was proposed by the Prosecution was that one should not allow the Tribunal or leave the Tribunal in an area of ambiguity, that when there is an examination, that the Defence may of course not proceed with the cross-examination. They may decide then to keep silent. And in that case, one must avoid any ambiguity. This is what we are proposing, that there be an examination and perhaps not have a cross-examination and then find ourselves with a Defence that reserves its right for a later time and may at that point explain its position to the Tribunal. So here we are, and we simply wish to understand what the strategy is and what type of means one is going to use. This is what we are proposing, without needing to look any further. If you will, this is the rule of transparency, where if we feel we need to go further -- for example, if we feel that a cross-examination may shed further light on the issue or perhaps the Defence may simply say that they wish to research the possibility of reserving this cross-examination for another time period for such and such a reason. I don't know what the Defence feels about this position, but I would like to have some response, if there is a response, from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Of course, Your Honour. I believe -- and I think that this proposal is based on the British practice -- obviously there are different types of situations, and I believe my colleague Sayers has addressed some of them. In principle, I believe that whether a witness should be challenged, if a counsel believes that the statement of the witness is not consistent with, let's say, a previously given statement or a previously given testimony or during the process of investigation, I believe that we need to challenge him and need to challenge him right away. In fact, we do this in cross-examination. However, we have different types of situations where only later, after the presentation of other evidence, we realise that this witness said inconsistent things and we failed to address those things. So it is when we identify inconsistencies, this is either with respect to his other statements or with other statements of other witnesses, I believe that we need to give him an opportunity to explain, to clarify this inconsistency before we ask that this evidence be thrown out. But I don't think that we should set a strict rule because we have different types of situations. There will be situations where we will not able, as Defence counsel, to immediately spot that this witness is not telling the truth or not the full truth. So in my view, the question is one of the economy of the proceedings because we may find ourselves in a situation where we have to recall a witness at another time. So I am prepared to bear that in mind as a guiding idea, but I am not inclined to have that set as a strict rule, a priori. And again, let me point out that I come from a different legal system. This is something that we live with. Obviously we can adapt our positions, but in our Rules, if I had not asked certain questions in cross-examination, the Trial Chamber cannot conclude that I agree with the testimony because the Trial Chamber in the end will be the one to say: "I don't believe such-and-such a witness for such-and-such reasons" or not, regardless of whether the other side had challenged him at the cross-examination or not. But obviously I would like to be able to challenge the witness, I would like to have that opportunity, and if I may assist you in any further ways, I am prepared to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, we'll hear you in reply, if you could keep an eye on the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall be very brief. Contact with witnesses, the suggestion that a defendant, for example, needs to be -- I think the word was "comforted" -- while giving his evidence and guided as to his testimony is one that is to some very concerning. A witness, once he starts, can of course be spoken to -- not necessarily by his lawyers; that's a matter of particular regimes -- but can be spoken to about matters not to do with his evidence. It is far better for the witness, and for the Court that he is left alone with his memory and his documents. The temptation to corruption of the evidence is overwhelming, and anybody who has seen examples of testimony before and after breaks where there has been contact with attorneys is somewhat embarrassed about the role of the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, it may not be advertant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The corruption of the testimony could be wholly inadvertent and wholly innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, sir. And of course the witness is bound to say, or even to say by implication: "How am I faring? What can I do better?" And it is so dangerous that that's why the Rule -- and these are not English rules; these are rules that are practiced widely throughout the world, as I understand it, in common-law jurisdictions, and they secure a safer trial. Incidentally, what's good for fact witnesses is also good for experts, in my respectful submission. Experts, although they come to the court with sometimes more credit than ordinary fact witnesses, sometimes leave court with considerably less credit. They are as corruptible, innocently or otherwise, by contacts with the interested parties as any other witness. The domestic problem referred to is really no problem at all. If the Defence choose not to make use of the Victims and Witnesses Unit, it's, of course, possible for someone else to deal with the domestic arrangements, not the lawyers. Indeed, you wouldn't really expect the practicing lawyers to be ringing up the hotels and getting them into the taxis, at least not in this case, as I would imagine. So it's our submission that the best course, in order that you can you have the most satisfactory evidence, is that once any witness takes the stand, he is not allowed or she is not allowed further contact with the lawyers until it's all over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the other issues are concerned, what's said is that this is a peculiar English rule -- or particular, perhaps I should say -- English rule in relation to the defendant giving evidence, and also cross-examination. You've set out the reasons in your brief for why you say it should be applied here. Is there really anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's nothing to add, except indeed to observe it's -- again, it's certainly not just an English practice. We've set out, I think, Spain and Germany as two of the locations, but it also applies elsewhere, South Africa and other places, but I've only identified some, for this reason: We're not here to do it by weighing which number of jurisdictions follow a course, just to simply show that there is a difference, and it's for this Tribunal to decide which is most apt and appropriate for its jurisdiction. But can I simply say this: Any practice that requires the trier of fact to ponder an additional possibility -- whether it's tailoring of evidence, accidental tailoring of evidence, contact with a witness that has led to the tainting of evidence, whatever it may be -- any practice that requires that additional element to be considered by the trier of fact is making the trier of fact's job much more difficult. It is introducing a wild card, and I'll deal with that as I come to the issue of cross-examination by the most simple and homely of examples, but which may apply in the case. Supposing a witness speaks of a meeting and puts one of the defendants -- let's be neutral: Defendant X -- at the meeting. It's an important meeting; X was there. The issue is never joined, namely that issue X wasn't there. Various things follow. The witness can't say, "Of course he was there, and what's more, I can prove it by this and this means." What a silly suggestion. The witness can't say, "Well, come to think of it, you might be right. Perhaps he wasn't there." On top of all that, the Prosecution, hearing the issue not being challenged, and facing the particular problems we face here, may decide not to call the other four witnesses who could have put the defendant X at the meeting. At the end of all the evidence, or at the beginning of the Defence case, whichever it may be, defendant X says: "I wasn't there." The trier of fact then has to say: "What would the witness have said if that had been raised with him or her? He might have dealt with it entirely satisfactorily. He might have dealt with it wholly unsatisfactorily. Now I don't know." It's a rule, this rule of cross-examination, widely applied in the common law as I understand it. Again, we're not doing it by weighing the jurisdictions that do and the jurisdictions that don't. But I can say that the case of Browne v. Dunn, which is probably not falling off the tongue of every English lawyer -- it was referred to me by someone else who in another jurisdiction, Canada, uses it as the rule that underpins the rule there. They knew about it. It is a rule that is actually quite easy of application and extremely helpful to the trier of fact, and it makes purpose to cross-examination which is otherwise simply, presumably, a vehicle for general discrediting of the witness, skirting the issues if it's convenient to do so. I don't think I have anything else to add. These matters are all plainly allowed for under the Rules, and in particular under Rule 90(G), "the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of truth," and to avoid the needless consumption of time. We would commend these Rules to the Court -- not these Rules, these approaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as to your motion in respect of C, cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- you say that this is a common-law approach. If it is a common-law approach, of course it has been developed through case law. I'm not aware that it has been actually reflected in any statutory form in any jurisdiction. What I want to ask is this: Why is it necessary to have a rule like this reflected in writing? The Prosecution bears the legal burden of proof to the requisite standard, and it is the function of this Tribunal, this Chamber, as the trier of fact, to determine on the basis of all the evidence presented, whether the Prosecution's case has been proved to the requisite standard. Similarly, in particular cases, it will have to decide in specific matters whether a matter has been proved. You say that it will make the life of the Chamber easier, but the degree of ease I think is not really a relevant matter. I mean, speaking for myself, I'm prepared to live with the difficulty that it entails; you know? And to live with the discretionary power which I think rests with the Chamber as the trier of fact in a situation such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Point number one, not covered by authority, as I set out in the motion, because it is so well understood that it is imposed as a rule by judges in civil and criminal matters automatically. The sanction for failure to apply the rules sometimes is the recall of the witness, sometimes is the inference against the party whose counsel has not put something it should have done, sometimes there's simply -- and frequently -- there's no sanction at all because it is a matter of oversight. And if I have missed interpretation, I dare say Judge May may be able to flesh that out. But that seems to me the general application of a rule so well understood that it doesn't need to be covered by authority because it is largely a matter of practice. As to the second point, yes, of course, the Court can live with any difficulties that it faces as a result of the Rules or that it chooses to face as a result of its interpretation of the Rules or orders it will or will not make. What we draw to your attention is that you have the power to require this method of interrogating witnesses under 90(G), that doing so will make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth in a way that the other method will not, the other method which again allows much more significantly, the possibility of trial by ambush. Further, for the reasons I have been at pains to advance throughout this case thus far, the rule can avoid the needless consumption of time. This is matter of great importance. Typically, in complex cases where there are a range of discrete issues that have to be established and dealt with, once you have established an issue on evidence that is not challenged, you are safe to move on, on the basis that that is effectively accepted or not challenged. And as a rule, that saves a huge amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose another way of thinking aloud about dealing with this, the point you make about the witness, the witness says: "'A' was at the meeting." Under the English rule, the Defence of "A" would be required to put to the Witness, "'A' was not at the meeting," if that's the case. And that's the Rule that you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- advocating now. And the reason you were advocating it, as I understand it, is you are saying one of the underpinnings of the Rule is it then becomes clear as to whether there is an issue on the fact. Also it gives the witness the opportunity to answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- whatever it may be. Another way, I suppose, of dealing with it in a Tribunal such as this, without a jury, is simply to ask the Defence: "Is it challenged that 'A' was at the meeting?", and expect an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the way that I think Your Honour did in the case to which you referred and which I had heard -- I think, or seen. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose, I mean, in order to manage the case, which is the important issue, we could perhaps get on without the Rule which you suggest, but requiring us to play a part in deciding where we want to find out whether there's an issue or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's certainly an alternative. The losers then are likely to be the cross-examiners because, of course, if the losers have a case to advance against a witness, all too frequently it is they who can take the benefit of the cross-examination on the point because the witness may yield or may break down or may show weakness that subsequently can be relied upon in argument. I should of course have made the point, it's in the motion, that's what sauce for the goose is indeed sauce for the gander. The Defence witnesses and the defendant himself, when cross-examined, should have the opportunity of dealing in cross-examination with all important parts of the Prosecutor's case, for the same reason or for one of those same reasons. It's not fair as against him, when all the evidence is closed, to say "Well, I really wasn't given a chance to deal with it"; isn't the proper inference for you to draw this, that, or the other thing? And the Defence are entitled to say, and typically do in cases where this practice obtains, "Well, what do you think of that, members of the jury or Your Honour? It wasn't even put to him, they didn't have the courage to advance it to him, and now they try and sustain it as an argument to you." So it is equality of arms, and it's fair all around. I don't think I can amplify -- I will deal with any questions. I don't think I can amplify what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Our time is limited. There are two motions further which we have to consider, both of them Defence motions. The first one is the motion to which you have not had the opportunity to respond. It's the 8th of March, for advance notice of Prosecutor's intent to offer evidence subject to exclusion under Rule 95, and it relates to any evidence attained in the searches in Vitez on the 23rd of September of last year. At the conclusion, they request the Prosecutor to provide two weeks' advance notice to offer such evidence. Is there any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are two things in this motion. I think one is that the timetable point -- which is not a point at all, and I said to my friends yesterday, why on earth didn't they pick up the telephone and ask me about it? I've established direct and effective lines of communication. Of course it's sensible that this argument, which may take some time and may be an argument of some importance, we have yet to discover, should be timetabled so as not to inconvenience witnesses, not have witnesses hanging around. And of course I'll calculate, when the first piece of material from the search warrant is likely to be the subject of an attempt to lead it in evidence, I'll notify everyone and we can timetable matters then. It may even be that the best time to deal with it is right at the beginning of the case, but give us a week or so to sort that out. It really doesn't need a motion to deal with procedural matters; it simply can be dealt with between counsel. As to the other matter which they raise, that is the requirement for an inventory. This is really something that was, I think, omitted from their earlier motion doesn't allow for a complete new motion. If they had simply said, "Well, we're sorry, we overlooked that. Can we raise this, and here's the discrete legal basis?" If there is one or merits basis for having an inventory, if they had put that in a separate motion, we would have responded to it. What we would now like is time to respond to simply that part of it, if we judge that a response is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you prepared to provide the inventory?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not at the moment, not the full inventory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you want time to respond to the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To that simple part of the motion, which is the only part which really -- possibly calling for a reply. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And your response would include, would it, indication of when argument would be suitable on the issue of the evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so, but I'm perfectly happy to continue with the negotiations with my learned friends by telephone, and we can fix those things up. I have to say, since I'm on my feet, that I'm unhappy to discover or return to the personalised -- (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm simply going to say I'm unhappy to discover that we've returned to the rather personalised approach to pleadings which I thought we had knocked out last year in an exchange between myself and my learned friends, the characterisations of the Prosecutor herself and so on in this motion are most undesirable in our submission. I'm not going to take any more time with it because I know we're pressed for time, but it is unfortunate in the extreme. And I venture to suggest that it is not entirely helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We would echo and deprecate any personalisation of these matters. They can be dealt with professionally without comment. So how long are you asking for to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got quite a lot to get done. I would ask three weeks, I think, if that's possible. It's a small issue, but I now have a lot of things to get dealt with through the team, and I would ask three weeks. (Conference with legal counsel)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Three weeks is conveniently the 1st of April, before the Easter break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know you've got one other motion to deal with, and Mr. Scott will be dealing with that. Can I just mention one other small point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me -- response 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And as far as the Defence are concerned, it can be raised in due course at some stage during the trial or at the beginning of the trial, but we'll give the Prosecution time to respond. And certainly, if we can timetable a hearing in such a way, if it's needed for the argument, if we have to have a hearing in such a way as not to inconvenience witnesses, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no problems with giving the Prosecution time to respond on that point. I might only add that we have no intention and did not think we had personalised the argument. This is a matter that we feel extremely strongly about, deeply, strongly about, and we have characterised what we believe are the implications of the actions of the Office of the Prosecutor institutionally. We had no intention of calling into doubt the bona fides of our learned colleagues in particular. Rather, however, we felt it necessary to spell out explicitly what we believed the consequences were of the positions institutionally being taken by the Prosecutor. And if we have offended the Chamber, I apologise. We will attempt to walk the line between effective and zealous advocacy for our client and any excess as best we can. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand -- what, one more motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more motion, two matters of administration relating to the translation order. Can I just deal with clarity now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The rules require translated statements, of course, into B/C/S or into the language that the accused understands, and that's our duty. It is not in respect of accompanying documentation, as we understand it, nor is it, in fact, our duty to translate the other way around. I think it is the registry's duty still to do that and I will be corrected under Rule 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will be governed by the Rules in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the prior testimony of accused, of course, the estimates I was able to give you today reflected the statements that are outstanding. Our understanding is that the registry are dealing directly with the Defence. Indeed, Mr. Smith will recall, when he had a problem in getting material from the registry, I interceded on his behalf with Mr. Jean-Jacques Heintz and I think achieved some effect, although he made it clear to me that transcripts were something with which I shouldn't be involved, certainly if there is any question of providing other than final-version transcripts. I also understand that the tapes of transcripts in B/C/S are, I believe, available, and so that is the solution to that problem. It is not our duty to translate. It would be, in a sense, absurd when tapes already exist of the testimony in the language concerned. It would be utterly absurd that the document come to us and then to be retranslated. A waste of resources in the extreme. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, we have gone beyond break time. I think if we sat for another quarter of an hour, we could dispose of all these matters. Is that all right, looking at those behind the darkened screens? Is that all right? We will sit for another quarter of an hour. Yes, Mr. Scott, what's the point, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it please the Court, Your Honour, only if the Court wants a response on the motion for release. I would assume you would want to hear from the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have set out in our brief the legal argument for the proposition that Rule 65 of the Tribunal's Rules violates settled principles of international law generally and of the Tribunal Statute and it does this by shifting the burden to an accused to demonstrate why he should not remain in detention and by further requiring that there be exceptional circumstances justifying his release which has been interpreted to date by Trial Chambers but not, I might say, by the Appeals Chamber, as a virtually irrebutable presumption in favour of the accused remaining in detention, pre-trial detention, pending and during trial. I will not go over those arguments. They are largely not responded to in the Prosecutor's brief. They have chosen, rather, to argue that the Rule does have a presumption and it must be enforced. We have also argued that there are adequate assurances that, if released, these defendants will appear for trial and that neither would pose any danger to a victim, witness, or other person, particularly under the conditions that we have been at some pains to suggest in our motion. There are now, it seems to me, and I alluded to this earlier, additional grounds constituting exceptional circumstances that call for the immediate pre-trial release of the defendants, and those are bound up in the position the Defence now finds itself in if it is to have both an expeditious trial and a fair trial. We have a tremendous volume of material to work with and deal with our clients between now and the time of trial and during trial, and despite the best efforts of the detention centre, the working conditions are quite difficult. It typically requires, by the time one has gone to the detention centre and checked all the way in, an hour perhaps, sometimes more, to get all the way in and get into work. One must do the same thing going out. The hours are as fulsome as they're able to provide but nonetheless necessarily restrictive. One is not physically able to cart in all of the documents in a case this large. When you're trying to work in a hurry, to put the case together, and the defendants in these cases, having lived through the four years of history, are one of the chief resources in the preparation of their own defence, it is extremely difficult to make that process work when you are in a hurry and when you are dealing with large volumes of material; and I would argue, Your Honours, that in addition to the other circumstances argued in our motion, that the posture the Defence now finds itself in constitutes exceptional circumstances and that in order for there to be a fair trial after 18 months of detention, these defendants should be released so that they may work with us in preparing their defence prior to and during the trial, and that that is essential to the fairness of the proceeding and the situation in which Defence has now been put. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, briefly, please -- I'm sorry, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just very briefly. I completely support the arguments set forth by my learned colleague Smith. In fact, we worked on the motion together. But let me just add one more thing after we have heard today. The last argument mentioned by my colleague Smith, that is, the quality of the defence, in order to improve the quality of preparations for trial, we need our clients to work with us together; and today, when we see the problems, that is, the problems that have arisen in the last two weeks, I think that I would have culled down to three pages what I find are the significant points, which is we have a huge volume -- we work a lot in the detention unit, but there are limits to what we can do. Progress has been made, but I don't think that we can work as well as we can, and we need to spend more and more time working as the trial draws closer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honour, on this issue, we don't get into an argument about what the international law, in terms of what it should be, but apply the established law, the established jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and as we stated in our papers, the four requirements, that it is the burden of proof of the Defence to meet on each of those, we submit, Your Honour, that the Defence, neither of the accused has, in fact, met any of those four requirements. There has not been a showing of exceptional circumstances, there has not been any satisfactory assurance given that these accused would return and would appear if released. I will cover some of these in slightly more detail. There is no showing whatsoever that these accused would not pose a threat or danger to victims or witnesses; and finally, there has been no showing that the host country is willing to undertake responsibilities that would arise from these accused being released from custody. If I'm not mistaken, there's been no communication or response to the Court from the host country. Your Honour, what's really at stake here, what underlies these arguments is much the same as what has been raised throughout the course of the day, that the new exceptional circumstance supposedly is the lack of discovery. As Mr. Nice said earlier, it's extremely important, and the Prosecution cannot possibly say this loudly and firmly enough, to say that we believe, save for the issues concerning translation, that we are absolutely and have been absolutely in compliance with the rules and orders of this Court. There has been no finding in this litigation to date, since the initial appearance, either by Judge Jorda's Chamber or by this Chamber, of any lack of compliance. So we simply again must state that firmly, that if there is an exceptional circumstance in this case, it is not based on any non-compliance by the Prosecution. In fact, Your Honour, I think this again goes to a number of the issues raised to date -- to all of Your Honours -- I submit to the Court this is one of the most thoroughly discovered cases in any jurisdiction at any time. These defendants and these Defence lawyers have had the benefit of a number of related cases which have been laid out on the public record for now some years. Some of these issues have now been tried two or three times. The very same witnesses have now appeared and testified publicly two or three times. It's a little bit, to use a more common example, would be a little bit like a multiple defendant bank robbery in our national jurisdictions where the bank robbers were tried sequentially concerning the same set of facts, and the third or fourth defendant stands up and says, "I don't know enough about what this case is about," when virtually much of the same case has been tried several times before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I don't want to interrupt you, but we have been over all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm moving on, Your Honour, but I think it is important -- it is not an exceptional circumstance that there is simply a lack of knowledge that would justify the release of these defendants at this late day when we have a trial that is basically one month away, that there are no exceptional circumstances, not based upon lack of discovery or lack of information which would justify the release. Your Honour, we have grave concerns about the witness issue. The Court knows, and we accept the fact -- we believe that the Court knows that we mean in good faith -- that we believe in good faith that these are serious issues. We can represent to the Court, as we have in the past, that there are many witnesses who, if the Court will allow, are very close on the fence, on the edge, whether they will come to The Hague to testify or not. Some of them change their minds on a daily basis. To release the accused from custody now would send exactly the wrong message to a number of the victims and witnesses who are still trying to decide whether they will come to The Hague and testify or not. Your Honour, there has again been no showing of any sufficient conditions or accommodation of conditions that would assure the appearance of these defendants. The fact that they initially appeared, while everyone can take notice of that, I submit to the Court that the calculations involved change over time, and while they may have appeared at one time, that is no assurance or reasoning that this close date, having been provided now detailed discovery and detailed knowledge of the Prosecution's witnesses and evidence, that that same determination, the same coming back and appearing for trial, there is no assurance whatsoever that decision would be made. We're close to trial. We should go forward, Your Honour. The Prosecution has done everything it can to move this case to trial. It would be, we submit, the wrong decision to release the defendants at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. This Trial Chamber, in our judgment, has discretion to exercise under Rule 65 and should exercise it. There is no Appeals Chamber decision, to my knowledge, on how Rule 65 is to be interpreted, and it should be interpreted to avoid illegality under international law and in the way in which we suggest in our briefs. As to host country consent, I know of no flat obligation that the defendant must provide that before the Court makes a decision. It seems to us not a useful exercise to attempt to get host country decision until there is a decision by the Trial Chamber that at least would be in order. Finally, Your Honour, this case now has been thoroughly discovered but the question is when, even as to the public material, as we have said over and over, and if the OTP is in compliance as an institution with the Rules here, and we believe they are not, then it seems to me the difficulty that both the Trial Chamber and the Defence find themselves in indicate that the discovery rules need to be changed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Smith just invoked something that I would have brought up. There is a technical issue. I think that today may be the last chance for me to verify this. We ask whether the accused could sit at the same desk with us. It would really be of crucial importance for our communication. This way we are limited to just exchanging little notes on paper, and this would really be of help. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider that and we will consider the other motions. I don't think there is any other matter left except to invite your attention to the timetable as it is set out. That, of course, is not set in stone, but it is what we propose to follow. Yes, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was only standing up so that you could address at least someone if you need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A courtesy. Very well. Well, that timetable, as I was saying, we will endeavour to follow, and we would invite the Prosecution to attempt to, as I said earlier, bring its case, or the bulk of it, by the recess. I know, of course, that it depends on others; it doesn't depend on you alone. Perhaps they might aim in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly shall. Thank you very much for the timetable. It is extremely thoughtful of you to spell it out so fully. I do recall one issue that I mentioned in a motion -- not issue, one point I raised in the motion about procedure, it doesn't require anything like an answer or anything of that sort today, but I did inquire of the Chamber effectively whether it had a view as to how it would like to deal with paper exhibits. I think I mentioned this. There are various possibilities. The exhibit list is being prepared and all these materials will come at the same time as the pre-trial brief. I have given an approximation, I think, of the quantity of material in total that would be wholly unmanageable on the bench. Various possibilities occur to me, one of which is having a core bundle of documents which grows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be a good idea to have a core bundle. It would be helpful. As to the numbering of the exhibits, it may be helpful if you start with a numbering and probably we would follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that we -- even if there are gaps in the event -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can discuss that with the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twelfth of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
